planting.note: Direct-sow or divide rhizomes in fall into a rain garden margin or seasonal swale that stays damp through spring but can dry somewhat by late summer.

directions: One of the tallest checkermallows, reaching six feet, this species gives strong vertical structure to wet meadow and rain garden plantings, with bright pink spikes from late spring into summer drawing bees and hummingbirds. Its thick taproot plus rhizomes make it long-lived and tolerant of seasonally wet soil other perennials reject. Its height and purple-tinged stems make it a good middle-to-back-of-border native for Pacific Northwest meadow plantings, paired well with sedges and camas.

planting.note: Plant only nursery-propagated seed or divisions from conservation-compliant growers into seasonally moist, unmown prairie or meadow soil; never wild-collect, since this species is federally threatened.

directions: A federally threatened Willamette Valley wet-prairie endemic with pinkish-lavender flower clusters from May into September, this species is valuable in native habitat and restoration gardens, with nursery-propagated stock genuinely and legally available so garden use directly supports conservation rather than depleting wild populations. It tolerates heavier soils better than many garden perennials. Because populations vary regionally, with Willamette Valley plants showing taller, open flower stalks and Coast Range plants more compact, straight-species seed lots can show real garden variability — a feature, not a flaw, for naturalistic plantings.
sources: Oregon Department of Agriculture species profile

planting.note: Mechanically scarify seed, then cold-moist stratify 4+ weeks before fall sowing into lean, well-drained, dry-summer soil in full sun; untreated seed germinates poorly.

directions: An airy pink-flowered Willamette Valley prairie native, this checkerbloom serves as a nectar source for the federally threatened Fender's Blue Butterfly, making it a genuinely high-value pollinator and conservation-garden plant. Unlike most garden mallows, give this one lean, well-drained, dry-summer soil in full sun — it is a dry-prairie specialist, not a wetland plant. Its taxonomic history is genuinely complex, having been treated at various times as a distinct species or as a subspecies of a related checkerbloom, so cross-reference before treating it as identical to differently-labeled nursery stock.

planting.note: Cold-moist stratify seed before fall sowing at a dappled-light woodland edge rather than deep shade or blazing open exposure.

directions: A California native suited to dry open woodland and serpentine-soil gardens where few showy perennials thrive, this checkerbloom carries pink flowers with pale veins from April through July. It is genuinely serpentine-tolerant, valuable for gardeners dealing with the low-nutrient, often droughty serpentine soils that defeat most ornamentals. Some floras still file this under a closely related species name, so check which name a seed source uses before assuming it's a different plant from existing checkerbloom stock already in the collection.

planting.note: Direct-sow with cold stratification, or divide rhizomes, into clay or salt-influenced soil; water regularly only to establish, then let it dry out by late summer.

directions: A coastal Oregon and Washington native well-suited to stabilizing dry slopes and clay banks, this checkerbloom carries glossy maple-shaped leaves and bright pink flower spires blooming an unusually long season from May into October. It tolerates clay and salt-influenced air better than most garden mallows, making it a strong choice for maritime Pacific Northwest gardens. Let soil dry out in late summer rather than keeping it constantly moist — overwatering shortens its lifespan compared to plants grown lean.

planting.note: Direct-sow onto bare, lightly raked soil in fall; resents transplanting from pots once past the seedling stage.

directions: A California-endemic annual with distinctive fringe-tipped pink petals, sometimes dark-based, this checkerbloom is easy to grow from direct-sown seed and well suited to annual wildflower meadow mixes and spring display gardens where perennial mallows would be too large or long-lived. Site in full sun in valley grassland, coastal prairie, or foothill woodland-edge conditions, and let it self-seed modestly in a bed left undisturbed over summer. Its deeply divided, bristly-hairy leaves and fringed petals distinguish it readily from the genus's more common perennial species already in cultivation.
